questions.question: What is the difference between throw and throws in Java?
questions.title: throw vs throws in Java
questions.direct_answer: **`throw`** is a statement that actually *raises* an exception object at runtime: `throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad id")`. **`throws`** is a clause in a method signature that *declares* the checked exceptions a method may propagate: `void read() throws IOException`. One creates and fires; the other warns callers. `throw` takes one exception instance; `throws` lists exception types.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can crisply separate the runtime action (throw) from the compile-time declaration (throws)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Mixing up the keywords or thinking throws actually raises the exception
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note throws is only required for checked exceptions; unchecked ones need no declaration

sections.title: One Letter Apart, Completely Different Jobs
sections.content:
`throw` and `throws` look almost identical but do opposite-side jobs. **`throw`** is an executable *statement* — it raises a specific exception object at runtime and immediately transfers control to the nearest matching handler: `throw new IllegalStateException("not ready")`.

**`throws`** is a *declaration* in the method signature. It tells the compiler and callers, 'this method may propagate these checked exceptions, so be ready': `String read(String p) throws IOException`. It doesn't raise anything by itself. Note `throws` is only needed for **checked** exceptions — unchecked (`RuntimeException`) ones never require it.

sections.title: throw vs throws
sections.content:
| Aspect | `throw` | `throws` |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | A statement (runtime action) | A clause in the method signature |
| Purpose | Actually raises an exception | Declares exceptions the method may propagate |
| Operand | One exception *instance* | One or more exception *types* |
| Example | `throw new IOException();` | `void f() throws IOException, SQLException` |
| Required for | Any exception you raise | Only *checked* exceptions you don't handle |

sections.title: Two Sides of the Same Coin
sections.content:
emerald|throw|~Runtime: raise it now|throw new XException()|takes one instance|jumps to handler
blue|throws|~Compile-time: declare it|method() throws A, B|takes type names|warns callers
amber|Checked only for throws|~Unchecked needs nothing|RuntimeException free|IOException must declare|or catch it
rose|Common slip|~Wrong keyword|throws doesn't raise|throw doesn't declare|keep them straight

sections.title: Without throws: checked exception not declared = compile error
With throw + throws used correctly
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`throw`** = runtime statement that raises one exception *instance*.
- **`throws`** = signature clause declaring exception *types* a method may propagate.
- **`throws` is required only for checked exceptions** you don't catch.
- **Unchecked exceptions never need `throws`.**
- **`throws` doesn't raise anything** — it's a warning to callers and the compiler.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: They're only one letter apart but they do completely different jobs, and they live on opposite sides of the process. Throw, without an s, is an executable statement. It actually raises an exception at runtime. You write throw, then a new exception instance, and at that point control immediately jumps to the nearest matching catch block, or propagates up if there isn't one. So throw takes a single exception object and fires it. Throws, with an s, is a declaration that goes in the method signature. It doesn't raise anything by itself — it just tells the compiler and anyone calling the method that this method might propagate these checked exceptions, so the caller needs to be prepared to either catch them or declare them in turn. So throws takes a list of exception types, not an instance. A clean way to remember it: throw is what you do, throws is what you warn about. One important nuance is that throws is only required for checked exceptions. If your method can propagate an I O exception and you're not catching it, you must declare throws I O exception, or the code won't compile. But for unchecked exceptions — anything extending RuntimeException, like IllegalArgumentException or NullPointerException — you never need a throws clause, even though you can still throw them. So in a typical method you might use both: a throw statement in the body to raise an unchecked exception when an argument is invalid, and a throws clause in the signature to declare a checked exception that a library call might propagate. The mistake to avoid is thinking throws raises the exception or that throw declares it — they're strictly the runtime action versus the compile-time declaration.

questions.question: Can you have a throws declaration without actually throwing that exception?
questions.title: throws Declaration Without Actual Throw
questions.direct_answer: Yes for **checked** exceptions — you can declare `throws IOException` even if the body never throws it; the compiler allows over-declaring, and callers must still handle it. For **unchecked** exceptions it's also legal but pointless. The catch: declaring a *checked* exception you never throw forces callers into needless handling, so don't over-declare.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand that throws is a contract the compiler permits to be broader than reality, and the downside of over-declaring
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Believing the compiler requires the body to actually throw every declared checked exception
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that over-declaring checked exceptions leaks an implementation detail and burdens callers; declare only what you really propagate

sections.title: throws Is a Contract, Not a Promise to Throw
sections.content:
You absolutely can write `throws IOException` on a method whose body never actually throws an `IOException`. The compiler treats `throws` as the **maximum** set of checked exceptions a method *may* propagate — it never insists the body actually throw each one. So over-declaring compiles fine.

The consequence is on the **caller** side: because the signature says the method *might* throw `IOException`, every caller must catch it or declare it themselves, even though it can never happen. That's wasted handling and a leaked, misleading contract. The rule: declare only the checked exceptions you genuinely propagate. (For interface methods, declaring a `throws` that implementations *might* need is a valid exception to this.)

sections.title: Over-Declaring throws
sections.content:
emerald|Allowed|~Compiler permits it|throws X without throwing X|throws = upper bound|not a requirement
rose|Caller pays|~Forced handling|must catch/declare X|even if impossible|noisy try-catch
amber|Interface case|~Legitimate|declare what impls may throw|base contract|e.g. close() throws Exception
blue|Rule|~Declare what you propagate|no more, no less|keeps contract honest|avoid leaks

sections.title: Legal but Wasteful Over-Declaration
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking the body must throw every declared checked exception.** `throws` is an upper bound, not a mandate.
- **Copy-pasting `throws` clauses** that no longer apply after refactoring.
- **Over-declaring `throws Exception`** 'just in case' — it forces blanket handling on callers.
- **Removing a `throws` that callers depend on** as part of a published API — that's a breaking change.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **You can declare a checked exception the body never throws** — the compiler allows it.
- **`throws` is the maximum set** a method may propagate, not a promise to throw.
- **Over-declaring burdens callers** with handling that can never fire.
- **Interface/base methods may declare** exceptions implementations might need.
- **Declare exactly what you propagate** to keep the contract honest.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Yes, you can have a throws declaration without the body actually throwing that exception, at least for checked exceptions. The compiler treats the throws clause as the maximum set of checked exceptions the method is allowed to propagate — it's an upper bound, not a requirement that the body actually throw each one. So if I write a method that just adds two numbers but I declare throws I O exception on it, that compiles perfectly fine, even though there's no way an I O exception could ever come out of it. The interesting part is the consequence, which falls on the caller. Because the signature advertises that the method might throw I O exception, every caller is now forced to either catch it or declare throws themselves, even though it can never actually happen. So you end up with dead try-catch blocks that handle an impossible case, which is just noise that makes the code harder to read and leaks a misleading contract. So while it's legal, over-declaring is a bad habit. The rule I'd follow is to declare exactly the checked exceptions you genuinely propagate — no more, no less. There is one legitimate exception to that, which is interface or base-class methods. There it can make sense to declare a broader throws clause that implementations might need, even if a particular implementation doesn't throw it. A classic example is AutoCloseable's close method declaring throws Exception, so that any implementation is free to throw whatever it needs. But for ordinary concrete methods, keep the throws clause honest and tight.

questions.question: Can a subclass method throw more checked exceptions than the parent method?
questions.title: Checked Exception Rules in Method Overriding
questions.direct_answer: No. An overriding method **cannot declare broader or new checked exceptions** than the method it overrides — it may declare the **same, narrower (subtype), fewer, or none**. This preserves the Liskov substitution guarantee: code calling through the parent type only handles the parent's declared exceptions, so a child can't surprise it with a new checked exception. Unchecked exceptions are unrestricted.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the override rule for checked exceptions — narrower or fewer, never broader or new
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking a subclass can add any throws it likes, or that the rule also restricts unchecked exceptions
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Tie it to substitutability: callers using the parent reference must not face exceptions they couldn't know about

sections.title: Overrides May Only Narrow Checked Exceptions
sections.content:
When you override a method, the override's `throws` clause must be **no broader** than the parent's for **checked** exceptions. You may declare the same checked exceptions, **subtypes** of them, **fewer** of them, or **none at all** — but never a **new** checked exception or a **broader** one.

Why? **Substitutability.** Someone holding a parent-type reference compiles against the parent's signature and only prepares for the parent's declared exceptions. If a child could throw a brand-new checked exception, that caller would be blindsided by something it never had to handle. This rule doesn't apply to **unchecked** exceptions — an override can throw any `RuntimeException` freely, since callers were never forced to handle those.

sections.content:

rose|Not allowed|~Broader or brand-new checked|parent throws IOException|child throws Exception ✗|compile error
blue|Why|~Liskov substitutability|caller sees parent signature|can't be surprised|by unknown checked Ex
amber|Unchecked is free|~RuntimeExceptions exempt|override may throw any|callers never declared them|no restriction

sections.title: Wrong: override widens the checked exception
Right: same, narrower, or no checked exception
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Adding a new checked exception** in the override — compile error.
- **Widening** (`IOException` → `Exception`) in the override — also a compile error.
- **Thinking the rule covers unchecked exceptions** — it doesn't; those are unrestricted.
- **Forgetting interfaces follow the same rule** when implementing a method.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Overrides may declare same, narrower (subtype), fewer, or no checked exceptions.**
- **They cannot declare broader or brand-new checked exceptions.**
- **The rule exists to preserve substitutability** (Liskov) for parent-type callers.
- **Unchecked exceptions are unrestricted** in overrides.
- **Interfaces and abstract methods** follow the same constraint.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: No, a subclass method that overrides a parent method cannot declare broader or new checked exceptions than the parent. What it can do is declare the same checked exceptions, or narrower ones — meaning subtypes of what the parent declared — or fewer of them, or even none at all. But it can never widen the set or introduce a brand-new checked exception that the parent didn't declare. The reason comes down to substitutability, the Liskov substitution idea. When some code holds a reference of the parent type and calls the method, it was compiled against the parent's signature, so it only prepared to handle the checked exceptions the parent declared. If a subclass were allowed to throw some new checked exception, that caller would suddenly be hit by an exception it never had any reason to handle, which would break the guarantee that a subclass can stand in safely for its parent. So the compiler enforces this. A concrete example: if the parent's read method declares throws I O exception, then an override can declare throws FileNotFoundException, because that's a subclass of I O exception, or it can declare nothing at all, but it cannot declare throws Exception, because Exception is broader than I O exception. The one thing this rule does not restrict is unchecked exceptions. An override is free to throw any RuntimeException it likes, because callers were never forced to handle those in the first place, so there's no contract to violate. And this same rule applies when you implement an interface method, not just when you extend a class.

questions.question: How do you rethrow an exception in Java?
questions.title: Rethrowing Exceptions in Java
questions.direct_answer: To rethrow, you `catch` an exception and `throw` it again — either the **same** instance (`throw e;`) to add no new info but log/act on it, or a **new** wrapping exception that **passes the original as the cause** (`throw new MyException("msg", e);`). Always preserve the cause when wrapping; never `throw new MyException("msg")` without it, or you lose the root stack trace.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know how to rethrow while preserving the original cause via exception chaining
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Rethrowing a new exception without passing the original as the cause, losing the root stack trace
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Java 7 'precise rethrow' lets you catch Exception and rethrow specific subtypes when the throws clause allows

sections.title: Rethrowing: Same Instance or Wrapped
sections.content:
Rethrowing means catching an exception and throwing it onward instead of fully handling it. There are two forms. **Rethrow the same instance** (`throw e;`) when you want to log or do partial cleanup here but let a higher layer handle it. **Wrap and rethrow** (`throw new DomainException("context", e);`) when you want to translate a low-level exception into a meaningful one for your layer.

The non-negotiable rule when wrapping: **pass the original exception as the cause** (the second constructor argument). That keeps the full chain so `getCause()` and the stack trace still point at the real culprit. Forgetting the cause is the classic bug that makes production failures undebuggable. Since Java 7, **precise rethrow** even lets you catch a broad type and rethrow its specific subtypes.

sections.title: Two Ways to Rethrow
sections.content:
emerald|Rethrow same|~throw e;|adds logging / cleanup|same type & stack|caller still handles it
blue|Wrap & rethrow|~throw new X(msg, e)|translate to your layer|MUST pass cause|getCause() recovers root
rose|The bug|~new X(msg) no cause|original lost|stack trace truncated|undebuggable in prod
amber|Precise rethrow|~Java 7|catch broad, throw specific|narrows throws clause|cleaner signatures

sections.title: Wrong: wrapping without the cause loses the root
Right: rethrow with the cause preserved
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Wrapping without the cause** — `new X(msg)` instead of `new X(msg, e)` drops the root.
- **Log-and-rethrow** — logging then rethrowing the same exception causes duplicate log entries up the stack.
- **Swallowing** — catching and not rethrowing when you can't actually handle it.
- **Changing the type for no reason** — only wrap when the new type adds meaning to your layer.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Rethrow the same instance** (`throw e;`) to act locally but defer handling.
- **Wrap and rethrow** to translate to a domain exception — **always pass the cause**.
- **`new X(msg, e)`**, never `new X(msg)`, when wrapping.
- **Avoid log-and-rethrow** duplication — log once at the boundary.
- **Java 7 precise rethrow** lets you catch broad and rethrow specific subtypes.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Rethrowing means you catch an exception but, instead of fully handling it, you throw it onward so a higher layer can deal with it. There are really two ways to do it. The first is to rethrow the same instance — you just write throw e. You'd do that when you want to do something locally, like increment a metric or log a bit of context or do partial cleanup, but you still want the original exception, with its original type and stack trace, to propagate up to whoever is better placed to handle it. The second way is to wrap and rethrow, where you catch a low-level exception and throw a new, more meaningful one for your layer — for example, catching a S Q L exception in the data layer and throwing your own domain exception. And the absolutely critical rule when you wrap is to pass the original exception in as the cause, which is the second argument to the exception constructor. That keeps the full chain intact, so later someone can call getCause to get back to the root, and the stack trace still shows the real culprit under a Caused by line. The single most common bug here is wrapping without passing the cause — writing new exception with just a message and dropping the original. When that fails in production, you've thrown away the actual reason, and it's nearly impossible to debug. I'd also mention precise rethrow, which Java 7 added: it lets you catch a broad type like Exception and rethrow the specific subtypes, and the compiler is smart enough to let your throws clause list just those specific types. And I'd avoid the log-and-rethrow anti-pattern, where you log at every layer and rethrow, because you end up with the same error logged five times. Log once, at the boundary.

questions.question: What does throws Exception on a method signature mean and why is it bad practice?
questions.title: throws Exception Anti-Pattern in Java
questions.direct_answer: `throws Exception` declares that a method may throw *any* checked exception — the broadest possible contract. It's bad practice because it's **uninformative** (callers learn nothing about what can actually fail), forces callers into **blanket `catch (Exception)`** handling, and **hides** the specific exceptions. Declare the precise checked exceptions instead (e.g., `throws IOException, SQLException`).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand why an overly broad throws clause is a poor API contract
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Defaulting to throws Exception to avoid listing specific exceptions, or to silence the compiler
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain it leaks abstraction and forces callers to catch-all, which then masks new exceptions you add later

sections.title: throws Exception: The Lazy, Leaky Contract
sections.content:
Declaring `throws Exception` says 'this method might throw literally any checked exception.' It's the broadest contract you can write, and it's almost always a code smell. It's **uninformative** — a caller can't tell whether to expect a file error, a parse error, or something else. It **forces blanket handling** — callers end up with `catch (Exception e)`, which also swallows unrelated problems. And it **hides change** — if you later add a `SQLException`, callers silently absorb it with no compiler nudge.

The fix is to declare the **specific** checked exceptions your method really propagates: `throws IOException, SQLException`. That's a precise, self-documenting contract that lets callers handle each case meaningfully.

sections.title: Why throws Exception Hurts
sections.content:
rose|Uninformative|~Says nothing useful|could be anything|caller can't plan|poor documentation
amber|Forces catch-all|~catch (Exception e)|swallows unrelated errors|hides bugs|loses precision
blue|Hides change|~Add SQLException later|caller absorbs silently|no compile nudge|surprises in prod
emerald|Fix|~List specific types|throws IOException, SQLException|self-documenting|caller handles each

sections.title: Wrong: broad throws forces broad catch
Right: declare the specific checked exceptions
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **`throws Exception` to silence the compiler** instead of declaring real types.
- **Pairing it with `catch (Exception)`** — the two reinforce each other's vagueness.
- **Letting it leak through layers** so every method up the stack also says `throws Exception`.
- **Using it on public APIs** — it's a vague, hard-to-evolve contract for consumers.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`throws Exception` = may throw any checked exception** — the broadest, least useful contract.
- **It forces callers into `catch (Exception)`**, which hides unrelated bugs.
- **It hides newly added exceptions** — no compiler nudge for callers.
- **Declare specific types** (`IOException`, `SQLException`) for a self-documenting contract.
- **Especially avoid it on public APIs** that others depend on.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Putting throws Exception on a method signature means the method is declaring that it might throw any checked exception at all — it's the broadest possible contract you can write. And it's considered bad practice for a few related reasons. The first is that it's uninformative. A caller looking at the signature learns nothing about what can actually go wrong — it could be a file error, a database error, a parsing error, anything. So it's useless as documentation. The second problem is that it forces callers into blanket handling. If the method declares throws Exception, the caller pretty much has to write catch Exception, and that catch-all is dangerous because it also swallows unrelated exceptions and even bugs you'd rather see fail. The third problem is that it hides change. Say you later add a S Q L exception inside the method — because the signature already said throws Exception, none of the callers get a compiler nudge to handle the new case, so they just silently absorb it, and you might only find out in production. The fix is straightforward: declare the specific checked exceptions the method genuinely propagates, like throws I O exception, S Q L exception. That makes the contract honest and self-documenting, and it lets each caller respond to each failure differently — maybe retry on the I O exception but roll back on the S Q L exception. It also tends to leak: once one method says throws Exception, everything that calls it ends up saying throws Exception too, and the vagueness spreads through the whole stack. So especially on public APIs, I'd always declare precise exception types rather than the catch-all throws Exception.

speakable_v2.hook: throws Exception compiles fine and saves you typing — so why do code reviewers flag it instantly? Because it quietly poisons every caller.

beats.text: Declaring throws Exception on a method means 'I might throw any exception ever.' It's the most generic possible declaration — it gives callers zero useful information about what can go wrong and forces them into catch(Exception e), which is far too broad.

Freshers write throws Exception to make the Java compiler stop complaining about unhandled checked exceptions. It works — the compiler is satisfied. But it defeats the entire purpose of checked exceptions, which is to communicate specific failure modes to callers.

items: No information — callers don't know what kind of failure to expect
Forces catch(Exception e) — too broad; might swallow RuntimeExceptions that should propagate
Breaks documentation — throws should communicate specific failure modes
SonarQube rule squid:S2093 flags this as a code smell
Exception: acceptable in main() and JUnit test methods where broad catch-all is intentional

beats.text: candidates miss: When a caller writes catch(Exception e) to handle your throws Exception, it also catches NullPointerException and IllegalArgumentException — bugs that should propagate and be fixed. The broad declaration causes bugs to be silently swallowed.

items: Using throws Exception in service or DAO methods — use specific types or unchecked exceptions instead.
Thinking throws Exception covers all bases — it just shifts the problem to every caller.

speakable_v2.cap: Always declare specific exception types; use throws Exception only in main() or test methods where it's genuinely acceptable.

questions.question: What is the difference between throwing a new exception and rethrowing the same exception?
questions.title: New Exception vs Rethrow in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Rethrowing the same exception** (`throw e;`) keeps the original type, message, and stack trace — use it to add logging/cleanup while letting a higher layer handle the unchanged error. **Throwing a new exception** translates it into a different (usually domain) type — use it to add meaning, but you **must pass the original as the cause** (`new X(msg, e)`) or you lose the root stack trace.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can choose between propagating the same exception and wrapping it, and know to preserve the cause when wrapping
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Wrapping in a new exception without the cause, or wrapping unnecessarily when the original was already meaningful
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the layer-translation rationale: wrap at boundaries to give callers a stable, meaningful exception type

sections.title: Same Exception vs a New One
sections.content:
Both are forms of letting an exception travel upward, but they serve different goals. **Rethrowing the same instance** (`throw e;`) preserves everything — type, message, and the original stack trace — and is right when you only want to *observe* the failure (log it, record a metric, release a resource) but defer real handling to a caller.

**Throwing a new exception** translates the error into a more meaningful type for your layer — turning a `SQLException` into an `OrderRepositoryException`, say. This is the **exception-translation** pattern used at architectural boundaries. The catch: you **must** pass the original as the **cause** so the chain (and root stack trace) survives.

sections.title: Rethrow Same vs Throw New
sections.content:
| Aspect | Rethrow same (`throw e;`) | Throw new (`new X(msg, e)`) |
|---|---|---|
| Type seen by caller | Original | New (domain) type |
| Stack trace | Fully preserved | Preserved *if* cause passed |
| Purpose | Observe, then defer handling | Translate to a meaningful type |
| Risk | Caller coupled to low-level type | Losing the cause if you forget it |
| Typical place | Mid-method logging/cleanup | Layer/architectural boundary |

sections.title: Choosing Between Them
sections.content:
emerald|Rethrow same|~Keep everything|throw e after logging|original type & trace|defer to caller
blue|Throw new|~Translate the meaning|domain exception|MUST chain the cause|stable boundary type
rose|Wrap pitfall|~Forgot the cause|new X(msg) only|root trace lost|always pass e
amber|Don't over-wrap|~Original was clear|wrapping adds noise|only translate at boundaries|keep it meaningful

sections.title: Wrong: new exception with no cause
Right: rethrow same OR wrap with the cause
When to Use Each
sections.content:
**Rethrow the same** when you're in the middle of a method and just need to log, record a metric, or release a resource before letting the original exception continue to a caller that genuinely handles it. Don't translate if the original type is already meaningful to callers.

**Throw a new exception** at **architectural boundaries** — e.g., a repository converting JDBC's `SQLException` into a stable `DataAccessException` so the service layer never depends on JDBC. This decouples layers and gives callers a consistent exception vocabulary. Always pass the cause so debugging stays possible.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Rethrow same** preserves type, message, and stack trace — for observe-then-defer.
- **Throw new** translates to a domain type — for layer boundaries.
- **Always pass the cause** when wrapping: `new X(msg, e)`.
- **Don't over-wrap** — translating a already-clear exception just adds noise.
- **Wrapping decouples layers** from low-level exception types.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Both are ways of letting an exception travel up the call stack, but they're used for different reasons. Rethrowing the same exception — literally throw e — preserves everything: the original type, the message, and the original stack trace. You'd do that when you only want to observe the failure at this point, maybe log it, increment a metric, or release a resource, but you still want the unchanged exception to reach a caller that will actually handle it. You shouldn't translate it if the original type is already meaningful to your callers. Throwing a new exception, on the other hand, is about translation. You catch a low-level exception and throw a different, more meaningful type for your layer — for instance, a repository catching J D B C's S Q L exception and throwing its own data access exception. This is the exception-translation pattern, and it's really valuable at architectural boundaries because it decouples the layers above from low-level details — your service layer never has to know that J D B C even exists. The one rule you can't break when you do this is to pass the original exception in as the cause, the second constructor argument, so the full chain and the root stack trace survive. The classic bug is wrapping without the cause, which throws away the actual reason for the failure. So my decision rule is: rethrow the same exception when you're just observing in the middle of some logic, and throw a new wrapped exception at layer boundaries to give callers a stable, meaningful type — but always chain the cause, and don't wrap just for the sake of it when the original was already clear.

speakable_v2.hook: Rethrow the original or wrap it in a new type? Pick wrong and you either leak your data layer or delete the stack trace. Here's the rule.

groups.heading: throw e — transparent rethrow
groups.text: You rethrow the exact same exception object. The original stack trace is fully preserved — callers and logging tools see exactly where it was first thrown. The exception type doesn't change. Use this when you want to observe an exception (log, metric) and pass it through unchanged.

groups.heading: throw new X(msg, e) — wrapping rethrow
groups.text: You create a new exception that wraps the original. The new exception has a fresh stack trace from the current line, but the original is preserved as the cause — accessible via getCause(). This is the right pattern for layer translation in a Spring service.

items: Use throw e when you just want to log and pass the same exception through — don't change the type.
Use throw new X(msg, e) at layer boundaries to translate exception types while preserving the cause.
Never use throw new X(msg) without the cause — that's the one pattern that loses information.

beats.text: production trap: In a Java 17 service that throws new ServiceException(message) without the cause, production logs show the ServiceException but the underlying SQLException is gone. The DBA asks which query failed — you can't tell them because the original error is lost.

speakable_v2.cap: Rethrow the same exception to be transparent; wrap with cause to translate types — the cause is mandatory for production debuggability.
